rationale: The student confuses a small factual detail ('bees are yellow') with the central overarching idea. A side-by-side comparison directly contrasts a main idea (the big umbrella topic) against supporting details (small facts) using clear, parallel examples.
intent: Compare 'Main Idea' vs 'Supporting Detail' side by side for Grade 2 readers. Define each simply (e.g., 'the big umbrella' vs 'one small raindrop/fact'), showing 2-3 contrasting pairs (e.g., about dogs helping people or trees giving us shade). Do not use the bees example from the current passage.

data.title: Main Idea vs. Supporting Detail
data.intro: When we read stories or books, we need to know what is most important. Let us learn about the big main idea and the small details that help it grow!

item1.name: The Main Idea
item1.description: The main idea is the big boss or the main point of the whole story. It tells us what the story is mostly about, like a big umbrella that covers everything.
item1.visualPrompt: A large, bright red umbrella with words about dogs helping people written across the top.
points: It tells the most important point of the story.
It is like a big umbrella that covers all the facts.
Example: Dogs help people do many important jobs every single day.

item2.name: The Supporting Detail
item2.description: A supporting detail is one small fact or piece of information. It gives us extra help to show why the main idea is true, like one small raindrop falling.
item2.visualPrompt: A small blue raindrop next to the umbrella, with a picture of a dog leading a blind person.
points: It is a small fact that gives extra information.
It helps prove or explain the big main idea.
Example: Some dogs help blind people walk safely across the street.

synthesis.mainInsight: The main idea and the supporting detail work together like a parent and a child. The big main idea gives the overall message, while the small details tell us more about it.
keyDifferences: The main idea tells what the whole story is mostly about, while a supporting detail is just one small fact.
The main idea is like a big umbrella, and supporting details are like the small raindrops under it.
keySimilarities: Both are found inside the same reading story or book.
Both work together to help us learn and understand new things.
synthesis.commonMisconception: Students often think that every fun or interesting sentence in a story is the main idea, when it is actually just a supporting detail.

whenToUse.item1Context: Use the main idea when someone asks you what the book or story is mostly about in one sentence.
whenToUse.item2Context: Use supporting details when you want to give a cool fact or proof to explain the main idea.

gates.question: True or False: The main idea is just one small fact, while a supporting detail is the big point of the whole story.
gates.rationale: That is false! The main idea is the big point of the whole story, like a big umbrella. A supporting detail is just one small fact that helps explain it.

gates.question: True or False: Both the main idea and the supporting details are found inside the same reading story and work together to help us understand.
gates.rationale: That is true! They are both parts of the story. The big main idea gives the main message, and the supporting details give the extra facts to back it up.

judgement.reasoning: The activity directly targets the student's exact misconception (confusing an interesting small detail with the overarching main idea). It contrasts the two concepts explicitly using kid-friendly metaphors (umbrella vs. raindrop) and provides a concrete example (dogs helping people vs. seeing-eye dogs). It steps back from multi-paragraph analysis to foundational concept clarity, uses a clear side-by-side conceptual representation instead of a text stimulus, and does not leak the bees passage.
judgement.verdict: A teacher would definitely use this detour right now because it clearly contrasts a broad main idea from a specific detail using intuitive 2nd-grade metaphors.
